paper_metadata.title: Enhancing Knapsack-based Financial Portfolio Optimization Using Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm

summary: The paper presents a QWM-QAOA knapsack formulation for portfolio selection over 2-8 stocks, using Qiskit/QASM simulation, IBM FakeWashington noise, and IBM Nazca hardware. Reported approximation ratios are 1.00 in the best noiseless cases, about 0.95-0.96 for p >= 3, 0.70-0.98 on the noisy fake backend, and as low as 0.51 on real hardware, against a classical best-known solution benchmark.

experiments.description: QWM-QAOA gate-based portfolio optimization for binary knapsack instances with 2 to 8 stocks, evaluated on simulator, noisy fake backend, and real IBM quantum hardware.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Walk Mixer QAOA (QWM-QAOA) with QFT-based feasibility oracle
algorithm.parameter_initialization: First layer initialized with Initialize(); subsequent layers use previously optimized parameters (γopt, βopt)

optimizer_settings.parameter_bounds: β adjusted to [0, mπ) for trotterized mixer; γ bounds not reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One binary variable per stock; portfolio selection encoded as bitstring x where 1 means include and 0 means exclude. Weights are set to 1 for all stocks and capacity is half the number of assets.
problem_formulation.objective_function: maximize R(x) = sum_i x_i E(R_i) subject to sum_i x_i w_i <= C
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Feasibility oracle Uf with QFT-based weight accumulation and multi-controlled-NOT feasibility check; quantum walk mixer restricts evolution to feasible states
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Phase Hamiltonian Hc encodes the value function v(x); exact Hamiltonian form not fully specified

problem_instance.description: Binary knapsack formulation of portfolio selection using historical stock returns from selected U.S. equities.

dataset_specification.benchmark_name: Best Known Solution (BKS) from classical knapsack solver
dataset_specification.preprocessing: Historical prices converted to daily returns; expected returns computed with Markowitz model; assets evaluated in subsets of size 2 to 8; weights fixed to 1; capacity set to half the number of assets

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Historical stock prices -> daily returns -> expected returns via Markowitz/PyPortfolioOpt -> binary knapsack instance with unit weights and capacity floor(n/2)
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Approximation ratio compared against classical BKS across portfolio sizes 2-8; evaluated under noise-free simulator, noisy fake backend, and real device; sensitivity analysis over p=1..5 and m=1..5

noise_model.noise_type: simulator noise model from IBM FakeWashington; real-device noise on IBM Nazca

implementation_details.transpilation_target: IBM Qiskit backend / IBM Nazca / FakeWashington
implementation_details.classical_solver: Best Known Solution (BKS) via classical algorithm; SHGO for parameter optimization
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Historical return extraction and expected-return estimation with Markowitz/PyPortfolioOpt
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measure probabilities and select optimal bitstring via OptimalChoice; compute approximation ratio against BKS

speedup_claims.baseline_method: Best Known Solution (BKS) / classical knapsack solver
speedup_claims.conditions: Empirical comparison only; no asymptotic speedup derived
speedup_claims.caveats: Paper reports approximation ratios and qualitative claims of efficiency, but does not prove a formal speedup over classical methods.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: not established; evaluated only on 2-8 assets
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No complexity analysis or crossover estimate reported; experiments use up to 17 qubits in the largest portfolio instance and a 127-qubit IBM Nazca device for noisy runs
limiting_factors: No asymptotic speedup or complexity advantage is proven
Comparison is against classical best-known solution, not a full end-to-end classical runtime benchmark
Real-device approximation ratios fall to about 0.51-0.55
Noise and gate errors dominate on hardware

notes: Hardware type is explicitly reported for QASM simulator, IBM FakeWashington, and IBM Nazca.
num_qubits is not given as a single total for the main experiment; inferred from the table as 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, and 17 qubits depending on portfolio size, with 17 as the largest reported.
Circuit depth p=3 is explicitly reported as the best-performing circuit layer.
No asymptotic speedup order is formally derived; the paper only reports empirical approximation ratios, so speedup_order is inferred as none_proven.
The paper states the use of Qiskit, QASM simulator, FakeWashington, and IBM Nazca, but does not provide gate counts or transpiled depth.

The paper reports high approximation ratios in noiseless simulation (up to 1.00) and 0.95-0.96 for p >= 3, but also substantial degradation on noisy fake backend (down to 0.70) and real IBM Nazca hardware (down to 0.51).
No practical quantum advantage over classical methods is demonstrated; the paper compares to a classical BKS benchmark only.
